definition: The amount of independent information represented by correlated or weighted observations.
example: Assess a set of importance-weighted samples.
caveat: Definitions depend on the estimator and dependence structure.

definition: A scalar by which a transformation scales a corresponding eigenvector.
example: Study curvature using Hessian eigenvalues.
caveat: Real matrices can have complex eigenvalues.

definition: A nonzero vector whose direction is unchanged by a linear transformation.
example: Find principal directions of a covariance matrix.
caveat: Scale and sign may not uniquely identify the vector.

definition: A model combining L1 and L2 coefficient penalties.
example: Fit sparse models with correlated predictors.
caveat: Its mixing and overall penalty strengths need tuning.

definition: A continual-learning method penalizing changes to parameters estimated important for earlier tasks.
example: Retain previous-task performance while adapting.
caveat: Importance estimates and task assumptions can limit effectiveness.

definition: An activation linear for positive inputs and exponentially shaped for negative inputs.
example: Train a network with negative activation outputs.
caveat: Negative-side saturation changes gradient behavior.

definition: A vector representation learned or constructed for an item, token, or concept.
example: Represent a document for similarity search.
caveat: Nearby vectors are meaningful only relative to the embedding objective.

definition: The number of coordinates in an embedding vector.
example: Use a 384-coordinate sentence representation.
caveat: More dimensions do not automatically mean better representations.

definition: A table of vectors indexed by discrete identifiers.
example: Look up a token's initial vector.
caveat: Input and output embedding matrices may be shared or separate.

definition: The coordinate space containing embeddings and their chosen geometry.
example: Compare documents using cosine similarity.
caveat: Distances may not align with every task's notion of similarity.

definition: Average or weighted loss over observed training examples.
example: Compute mean training loss.
caveat: Training risk can underestimate deployment risk.

definition: Selecting a model to minimize loss on observed training data.
example: Fit a classifier by average cross-entropy.
caveat: Minimizing training loss alone can overfit.

definition: A component converting inputs into internal representations.
example: Encode a document for classification.
caveat: The term applies beyond Transformer architectures.

definition: A model with an input encoder and an output-producing decoder.
example: Translate text using cross-attention.
caveat: Not every generative model has a separate encoder.

definition: A model centered on an encoder producing contextual input representations.
example: Build embeddings or classification predictions.
caveat: It is not usually a standard left-to-right generator.

definition: Jointly training a mapping from raw or minimally processed input to final output.
example: Learn speech transcription directly from audio.
caveat: End-to-end systems can still contain preprocessing.

definition: Combining multiple models to improve predictions or robustness.
example: Average several independently trained classifiers.
caveat: Highly correlated errors limit gains.

definition: Mapping a text mention to a specific entity in a knowledge base.
example: Resolve an ambiguous organization name.
caveat: Recognition of a name does not identify the correct entity.

definition: Expected uncertainty or information content under a probability distribution.
example: Measure how spread out token probabilities are.
caveat: High entropy does not necessarily mean useful diversity.

definition: An objective term encouraging a policy to remain less deterministic.
example: Promote exploration during policy optimization.
caveat: More entropy is not always useful exploration.

definition: The system an agent interacts with, receiving observations and producing consequences and rewards.
example: A game, simulator, or tool-enabled task setting.
caveat: The environment can include other agents and hidden variables.

definition: A marker indicating a sequence or generation should end under the model's convention.
example: Stop decoding after an EOS token.
caveat: Chat formats may distinguish end-of-turn and end-of-sequence markers.

definition: A trajectory segment ending at a defined terminal condition.
example: One complete game or task attempt.
caveat: Some tasks are continuing rather than episodic.

definition: Stored records of particular interactions or events used by an agent.
example: Recall the outcome of an earlier tool attempt.
caveat: Borrowed cognitive terminology does not imply human-like experience.

definition: Uncertainty caused by limited knowledge, data, or model specification.
example: Identify poorly supported input regions.
caveat: Approximate estimators may fail under distribution shift.

definition: One pass through a specified training dataset.
example: Train for three complete passes.
caveat: Streaming or resampled datasets may not have a natural epoch.

definition: Selecting a random exploratory action with probability epsilon and a greedy action otherwise.
example: Explore in a discrete-action value learner.
caveat: Uniform random exploration may be inefficient or unsafe.

definition: Equality of true-positive rates across relevant groups under a common fairness definition.
example: Compare detection among truly positive cases.
caveat: This is a technical fairness criterion, not the full everyday concept.

definition: Equality of true-positive and false-positive rates across groups under the chosen setup.
example: Compare both error-related rates across groups.
caveat: It may conflict with calibration when prevalence differs.

definition: The straight-line distance between coordinate vectors.
example: Find nearest image embeddings.
caveat: Feature scaling changes the resulting geometry.

definition: Recognition or inference that an interaction is part of a test or evaluation.
example: Check whether benchmark cues change behavior.
caveat: Awareness does not automatically imply deceptive conduct.

definition: Variation in measured results caused by sample choice, random seeds, generation, or judging.
example: Repeat evaluations to estimate uncertainty in model comparisons.
caveat: A single score can conceal substantial uncertainty.

definition: A systematic tendency in an evaluator that affects scores independently of the intended quality criterion.
example: Check whether a judge favors its own output style.
caveat: More evaluations do not remove a systematic bias.

definition: The extent to which an evaluation process remains independent, uncompromised, and faithful to its intended criterion.
example: Prevent evaluated agents from editing their test results.
caveat: An accurate evaluator is still vulnerable if the system can manipulate it.

definition: An optimizable lower bound on log evidence, balancing expected data fit against divergence from a prior.
example: Train a variational autoencoder.
caveat: A tighter bound is not automatically a better downstream representation.

definition: The fraction of outputs matching reference answers under stated normalization rules.
example: Score short-answer questions.
caveat: Valid paraphrases can be marked wrong.

definition: A probability-weighted average of a random quantity.
example: Compute expected reward under a policy.
caveat: An expectation need not be a likely individual outcome.

definition: Alternating latent-variable expectation calculations with parameter optimization.
example: Fit a Gaussian mixture model.
caveat: EM generally converges to a local solution.

definition: A binned summary of differences between predicted confidence and empirical correctness or frequency.
example: Summarize confidence calibration.
caveat: ECE is sensitive to binning and can miss localized miscalibration.

definition: Expected loss over the target data distribution.
example: Reason about average future prediction error.
caveat: The true distribution is usually unknown.

definition: Recording configurations, metrics, artifacts, and context for training or evaluation runs.
example: Compare reproducible experiments.
caveat: Logged metrics are only meaningful when evaluation conditions are comparable.

definition: A subnetwork specialized or selected within a mixture-of-experts system.
example: One feed-forward expert processes routed tokens.
caveat: An expert's specialization is learned and may not be human-interpretable.

definition: The token-processing budget allocated to an expert for a batch or routing interval.
example: Limit per-expert token assignments.
caveat: Capacity limits and overflow handling vary by implementation.

definition: Placing different mixture-of-experts experts on different devices and routing token representations between them.
example: Distribute a sparse expert model.
caveat: Routing traffic and load balance are central costs.

definition: Methods producing understandable descriptions or evidence about model outputs or behavior.
example: Provide a local feature-attribution explanation.
caveat: A readable explanation need not reflect the actual mechanism.

definition: A regression metric comparing residual variance with target variance.
example: Summarize variability left unexplained by predictions.
caveat: It can differ from R² when residuals have a nonzero mean.

definition: Balancing information-gathering actions against actions with high current estimated reward.
example: Try an uncertain action versus a known good one.
caveat: Exploration can incur real costs or risks.

definition: A schedule reducing a quantity multiplicatively over time.
example: Multiply learning rate by a fixed factor periodically.
caveat: Fast decay can halt useful learning too early.

definition: Mismatch between training on reference histories and generating from a model's own earlier outputs.
example: Errors accumulate during autoregressive generation.
caveat: The term names one mismatch, not every generation failure.

definition: The range of functions or distinctions a model family can represent.
example: Compare the representational limits of two architectures.
caveat: Representability does not imply that training will find the representation.
